newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican criticises Helms-Burton law on Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Vatican criticises Helms-Burton law on Cuba.

text.p: The Vatican added its voice on Friday to widespread criticism of Washington's Helms-Burton law that penalises foreign firms doing business with Cuba.
"It is a law that involves extra-territorial application in a way which is legally very questionable," one of the Vatican's most senior cardinals, Roger Etchegaray, told Vatican radio.

Etchegaray, head of the Vatican's Justice and Peace Commission, noted that the legislation had been criticised not only in Latin America and among Western allies of the United States but also by Roman Catholic bishops in Cuba itself.

"Any economic measure which aims to isolate the country by eliminating the possibility of development and even threatening the survival of the people is unacceptable," Etchegaray quoted the Archbishop of Havana, Cardinal Ortega y Alamino, as saying.
Etchegaray added: "The Holy See is concerned by the appearance of attitudes which run counter to the principle of solidarity, which should be of particular inspiration in any policy regarding food."

The Helms-Burton law, which has been condemned by all major U.S. trading partners, including Canada and Mexico, allows U.S. citizens to sue foreign firms which invest in property confiscated after Cuba's communist revolution in 1959.
Etchegaray made his remarks in an interview about the World Food Summit in Rome, which Pope John Paul will open on November 13.
Cuban President Fidel Castro is among heads of state and government whom the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation has invited to attend the five-day gathering.
Though Castro has yet to confirm he will come, Archbishop Ortega told Reuters last week that he thought the Cuban leader would see the Pope for an historic first meeting if he did so.

A Vatican delegation led by the Holy See's "foreign minister", Archbishop Jean-Louis Tauran, is due in Cuba from October 25 for a visit which diplomatic sources say could pave the way for a meeting between Castro and the Pope.
Washington has portrayed Helms-Burton as a tool to help bring about a switch to democracy in Cuba, which has been subject to a U.S. trade embargo for three decades.

Etchegaray, without specifying the embargo on Cuba, repeated the Vatican's opposition to unbridled use of sanctions as a means of diplomatic pressure particularly when they threatened a country's food supplies.

"For the Holy See...sanctions represent a means of pressure on governments which do not respect fundamental principles of international co-existence and are to be used according to strict legal and ethical criteria," he said.
"But when they hit the civilian population indiscriminately, above all those who live in precarious conditions, they cannot be justified," he said.
